entries.markdown:
# Reading a Build Log Without Trusting It

## Why this note exists

A build log is a claim about what happened, written by the thing that did it.
That makes it useful and makes it the wrong place to look first when the claim
and the artifact disagree. What follows is the order that has held up.

## Start from the artifact, not the report

The artifact is the only thing a reader will ever receive. Ask it directly:

```bash
find dist -name "*.html" | wc -l
du -sh dist
```

If those two numbers surprise you, nothing in the log matters yet.

## Count what shipped, then count what was meant to ship

### The two numbers, and which one lies

A build that publishes fewer pages than it discovered is doing its job. One
that publishes more has a defect with no message attached to it.

```bash
ls dist/notes | wc -l
```

## Read the compressed members too

### Why a plain text search is not enough

A search index is usually gzip, so a plain text search over the output is blind
to the largest file in it:

```javascript
const raw = readFileSync(fragment);
const text = gunzipSync(raw).toString("utf8");
```

This is the single most common way a scan reports clean over something it never
read.

## Check the shape, not one instance

One page proves one page. A property holds when it holds over the set:

```bash
for page in dist/notes/*/index.html; do
  printf "%s %s
" "$(wc -c < "$page")" "$page"
done | sort -rn | head
```

A distribution with a floor tells you something different from one with a long
tail. A floor is fixed cost on every page; a tail is one page doing something
unusual.

## When the numbers disagree with the log

Believe the filesystem. A log line is produced by code that may be measuring the
wrong thing — the whole reason to look at the artifact first.

```bash
git status --short
```

A dirty tree is the commonest explanation for a result nobody can reproduce.

## What this does not cover

Timing, memory, and anything requiring a second machine. Those need a benchmark
rather than a reading, and a benchmark that runs once is an anecdote.
